facts.claim: On the trek from Lukla to Base Camp, the first hazard is altitude sickness: the trek's slow gain in altitude is meant to avoid it.

versions.note: The trek gives climbers time to acclimatize properly and avoid altitude sickness.

source.title: Nepal Nomad: Everest Expedition

versions.note: The rest day in Dingboche and the stop in Lobuche, at 4,910 m, are for acclimatization, as the air holds less oxygen.

source.title: Tidy Himalaya: Everest Expedition

facts.claim: The trek to Base Camp is the first acclimatization: gain altitude slowly, with rest days on the way.

versions.note: The trek takes about 10 days, and gives time to acclimatize gradually.

source.title: Alpine Ascents: Everest itinerary

versions.note: A rest day in Dingboche, and a stop in Lobuche before the last push to Base Camp.

facts.question: Where on the trail from Lukla to Base Camp do trekkers fall or get hurt, and how often? None of the sources read names a hazard of the trail itself.

facts.claim: Base Camp can be hit by avalanches from the slopes around it: in the 2015 earthquake, one from Pumori swept through the camp and killed at least 18 people.

versions.note: The avalanche came from Pumori, next to Everest; 18 killed, several badly hurt, the upper part of the camp hit hardest.

source.title: National Geographic: Everest Base Camp a 'War Zone' After Earthquake Triggers Avalanches (2015)

versions.note: A collapsed serac on Pumori destroyed 40 to 50 percent of Base Camp; at least eighteen dead and several dozen hurt.

source.title: Alpinist: Nepal's Earthquake Aftermath (2015)

facts.claim: Base Camp is home for weeks: climbers rest and recover there between rotations to the higher camps, eat well, and see a doctor at the Everest ER.

versions.note: Home for several weeks, an important place to rest and recover; the cooks' meals; a visit to the Everest ER in the first few days.

source.title: Alpine Ascents: Everest itinerary

versions.note: A few weeks at Base Camp to acclimatize, with rest periods between the rotations to Camps 1 to 4.

source.title: Nepal Nomad: Everest Expedition

versions.note: At least 50 days at Base Camp, resting and preparing for the climb.

source.title: Tidy Himalaya: Everest Expedition

facts.question: Which illnesses go round Base Camp (a cough, the stomach), and how do climbers avoid them? None of the sources read names one; Alpine Ascents only sends its climbers to the Everest ER.

facts.claim: In the Khumbu Icefall, seracs and ice from the West Shoulder fall without warning, avalanches come down, deep crevasses open under thin snow, and the moving glacier shifts the ladders.

versions.note: Ice falling off the West Shoulder is widely considered the most pressing danger in modern times; crevasses over 45 m deep and seracs over 9 m high; the Icefall can move a metre a day and shift suddenly, dropping or bending ladders.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2023: First Deaths of Season

versions.note: A constantly shifting glacier with deep crevasses and towering seracs; avalanches and seracs threaten to fall; steeper ladders near the top.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

versions.note: One of the riskiest parts of the route, for its seracs, crevasses and shifting slabs of ice.

source.title: Nepal Nomad: Everest Expedition

versions.note: In 2014, sixteen Sherpa, Tamang, Gurung and Nepali high-altitude staff died in a single ice avalanche in the Icefall.

source.title: Alpinist: Nepal's Earthquake Aftermath (2015)

versions.note: On 12 April 2023, at 04:00 and 5,700 m, three Sherpas died in a serac accident in the Icefall.

source.title: Explorersweb: 2023 Everest Deaths Totaled 18, the Worst Ever

facts.claim: Go through the Icefall early, before the sun warms the ice, don't linger in it, and stay clipped to the fixed ropes, on the ladders too.

versions.note: Climbers pass in the early morning, when the ice is stable; the danger is highest in the afternoon, when the sun hits the seracs. Always be clipped to the fixed rope, ladders included: many falls into crevasses came from not being clipped in.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2023: First Deaths of Season

versions.note: Climbers set out before sunrise, before the glacier warms.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

facts.claim: The route from Base Camp to Camp 1, through the Khumbu Icefall, is this long.

versions.note: 1.62 miles, in the table of the South Col route's camps.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Comparing the Routes of Everest, 2026 Edition → C1

versions.note: 1.62 miles, in the Quick Facts.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest → Quick Facts

versions.note: 2.5 miles: the Icefall itself, where the glacier drops out of the Western Cwm, in the post's description of it; the post gives no figure for the route.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2021: Everest's Gatekeeper, the Khumbu Icefall

facts.claim: The scale every section of the route is drawn at: how many real metres a drawn metre of its length and its rise stands for, with its walls, crevasses and ladders at life size, so that a fall reads true. The mountain's clock runs faster than this (time.compression), and the climber goes faster than in life over the drawn ground by as much, so a section still takes its real hours. Fitted to the Icefall, Base Camp to Camp 1: 280 m of ground rising 45 m stand for its length and its rise.
The Icefall's slopes run from this gentle to this steep, with the walls between them climbed on ladders.

versions.note: From steep 60-degree climbs to gentler 20-degree slopes, often with long ladders to cross; the final section has steeper ladders and sharper grades, and at the top the terrain levels out into the Western Cwm, with Camp 1 half an hour to an hour on.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest → Section 1: Khumbu Icefall to Camp 1

facts.claim: The Icefall Doctors fix the route through the Icefall with this many ladders in a season, across the crevasses and up the walls.

versions.note: Only 21 ladders were used to open the route to Camp I in 2017, on a line that takes about an hour longer than the traditional one.

source.title: The Himalayan Times: Icefall doctors open Everest route, Base Camp being set up (2017)

versions.note: More than 20 aluminium ladders, with ropes, in 2018, on the central traditional route, which has more blue ice but less hanging glacier.

source.title: The Himalayan Times: Icefall doctors open 'safest' Everest route (2018)

versions.note: Eight ladders across three sections when the route opened on 28 April 2026, with more likely as the crevasses widen; a serac about 55 m long, 28 m high and 37 m wide, with several cracks, hung over the route's critical section.

source.title: The Himalayan Times: Khumbu Icefall route opened, but risks persist: SPCC (2026)

facts.claim: Where one ladder isn't long enough, the Icefall's ladders are lashed together end to end, three, four or more, and a long one sags in the middle and bounces; they go across, up, down and at an angle.

versions.note: How many ladders are lashed together? Not too bad if only one, but three, four or more, it sinks in the middle, it bounces. They go down, straight up and at an angle, almost never straight across; dual ladders in high-traffic areas; the safety line is tied to an ice screw across the crevasse, and climbers clip into both lines.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2013: Crossing the Ladders of Everest

facts.claim: A climber's own kit for the Icefall includes steel 12-point crampons, a harness that fits over all their clothing, a headlamp with freshly installed batteries and spares, and two one-litre water bottles in insulated covers.

versions.note: Modern steel 12-point crampons with anti-balling plates; a harness that fits over all clothing with adjustable leg loops; a headlamp with freshly installed batteries plus spare batteries, rental headlamps including no spares; two one-litre hard-sided water bottles, with insulated parkas that fully enclose them.

source.title: Alpine Ascents: Mount Everest Expedition Gear List

facts.claim: From Base Camp the route crosses to Crampon Point, then climbs the lower Icefall, the Popcorn, the flat Football Field about halfway up and the steeper Upper Icefall, to the flat snow at its top that leads into the Western Cwm and on to Camp 1.

versions.note: Crampon Point is the last flat section, where climbers attach their crampons; the first section is a continuous climb that undulates wildly, with the first ladder after an hour and huge seracs teetering above; then the section known as the Popcorn; then the Football Field, a large area of flat hard-packed snow, about halfway up, after two or three hours the first time; then the Upper Icefall, whose final section always has steeper ladders and sharper grades; at the top, a flat expanse of snow leads into the Western Cwm, with Camp 1 half an hour to an hour on.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Mt. Everest South Col Route Maps

facts.claim: The Football Field, the flat in the middle of the Icefall, lies at this altitude, and it is the part most exposed to falling seracs.

versions.note: The serac accident of April 2023 struck as the climbers were crossing the so-called Football Field at 5,700 m, the section in the middle of the Icefall most exposed to falling seracs.

source.title: Explorersweb: Cause of Everest Tragedy Remains Unclear (2023)

facts.claim: Base Camp's tents stand on the Khumbu Glacier itself, on ice covered in dirt and rocks, not on snow.

versions.note: The moving river of ice under Base Camp is covered in dirt, and carries rocks down from high in the Western Cwm; a steep path leads down onto the glacier.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest Base Camp (2011)

versions.note: Base Camp sits on the Khumbu Glacier, and the ice underfoot melts much faster in the climbing season; the authorities thought of moving it to the top of a lateral moraine.

source.title: Explorersweb: Will Everest Base Camp Move Next Spring? (2022)

facts.claim: In the Western Cwm, hidden crevasses lie under thin snow bridges, and on a clear, windless day the heat is scorching.

versions.note: Hidden crevasses under thin snow bridges; the walk from Camp 1 to Camp 2 can be scorching, up to 100 degrees Fahrenheit.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

versions.note: Huge lateral crevasses in the middle of the valley; scorching on a clear, windless day.

source.title: Nepal Nomad: Everest Expedition

facts.claim: Cross the Western Cwm early in the morning, before the heat.

versions.note: The heat encourages climbers to leave early in the morning.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

facts.question: How do climbers keep from drying out and overheating in the Western Cwm: how much water, what pace, what clothes? The sources read name only the heat and the early start.

facts.claim: The Lhotse Face is steep, hard ice where a slip ends badly, and the climb to Camp 3 exhausts and dries out the climber.

versions.note: Only about 30 degrees, but it seems to become vertical; the crampons don't bite the ice as quickly as you'd like; a slip there ends badly.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2018: Inside the Mind During the Last Rotation

versions.note: Considerable risks; climbers battle exhaustion, dehydration and steep terrain on the way into Camp 3, and a storm can erase the kicked steps.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

versions.note: The route to Camp 3 is steep and icy.

source.title: Tidy Himalaya: Everest Expedition

versions.note: A steep face, a climb of 1,000 m to the South Col.

source.title: Olaf Rieck: Everest, the route

facts.claim: Climb the Lhotse Face on the fixed ropes with a jumar, stay clipped at all times, at Camp 3 too, and keep one device on the rope when passing an anchor.

versions.note: Always have one device clipped to the fixed rope; at the end of a rope, the jumar comes off and goes on the next one.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2018: Inside the Mind During the Last Rotation

versions.note: Climbers stay clipped to the fixed line at all times, even at Camp 3.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

versions.note: Camp 3 is reached by ascending fixed ropes.

source.title: Tidy Himalaya: Everest Expedition

facts.question: Do climbers queue on the Lhotse Face's fixed ropes, and what does it cost them? The spec says so; none of the sources read does.

facts.claim: From Camp 3 to the South Col, past the Yellow Band and the Geneva Spur, climbers enter the death zone: extreme cold, hurricane-force winds, and an altitude where the body can't rest.

versions.note: The Geneva Spur and the Yellow Band, two large obstacles; at the South Col and Camp 4, climbers enter the death zone.

source.title: Mountain Project: Southeast Ridge (South Col) of Everest

versions.note: Steep from Camp 3; the South Col is harsh weather and destructive altitude, the death zone, where altitude sickness can kill, sleep is hard and digestion slows or stops.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

versions.note: Notorious for extreme cold and hurricane-force winds.

source.title: Tidy Himalaya: Everest Expedition

versions.note: At the South Col, climbers enter the deadly zone.

source.title: Nepal Nomad: Everest Expedition

facts.claim: Above Camp 3 climbers breathe supplemental oxygen, and at the South Col they decide to go or not: the window is a few days, and if the weather doesn't allow, they descend.

versions.note: Most climbers rely on supplemental oxygen from Camp 3; the window at the South Col is two or three days, and without the weather climbers descend, often to Base Camp.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

versions.note: Supplemental oxygen from Camp 2, not Camp 3.

source.title: Alpine Ascents: Everest itinerary

versions.note: If the weather isn't clear, with low winds, climbers must descend in these few days.

source.title: Nepal Nomad: Everest Expedition

versions.note: A safe summit push needs four to seven days of summit winds under 48 km/h; a day's wait to see the doctors for the go or no go.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2018: Inside the Mind During the Last Rotation

facts.claim: On the summit push, from the Balcony past the South Summit and the Hillary Step, climbers face the altitude, the cold, frostbite, queues while their oxygen runs low, and corniced ridges over the Kangshung Face.

versions.note: Hundreds of climbers bottlenecked on the summit ridge; they turn their oxygen down so as not to run out, and can't move fast enough to stay warm; without supplemental oxygen, frostbite and altitude sickness are likelier.

source.title: National Geographic: Traffic Jams Are Just One of the Problems Facing Climbers on Everest (2019)

versions.note: Steep to the South Summit, with bottlenecks up and down; the most exposure on the ridge, and vertigo on the soft edges of the boot tracks.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

versions.note: Severe exposure on the ridge, past big snow cornices, with a risk of avalanche; a loose, rocky stretch with a tangle of fixed ropes after the Hillary Step.

source.title: Nepal Nomad: Everest Expedition

versions.note: In 1996, ropes not fixed in time at the Balcony and the Hillary Step bunched climbers up as their oxygen ran low; a whiteout with winds over 100 km/h followed, and on the north side, severe frostbite.

source.title: Explorersweb: The 1996 Everest Tragedy, 30 Years Later

versions.note: In May 2024, a line of about fifty climbers at the Hillary Step broke a soft cornice over the Kangshung Face; several fell and were held by the fixed rope, two have not been found.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Weekend Update May 25: Season nears the End with Summits and Death

versions.note: Most of 2023's eighteen dead, many between 8,400 m and 8,760 m, died as altitude, exhaustion and cold wore them down.

source.title: Explorersweb: 2023 Everest Deaths Totaled 18, the Worst Ever

facts.claim: Start very early, turn around at the set time whether or not the summit is reached, keep enough oxygen for the way down, and judge yourself honestly: summit fever kills.

versions.note: In 1996 everyone was to turn around by 2 pm, to be back at the high camp before dark, and many ignored it; so close to the top, summit fever set in and common sense was ignored.

source.title: Explorersweb: The 1996 Everest Tragedy, 30 Years Later

versions.note: Going on to the summit without enough oxygen to get back down is poor decision making.

source.title: National Geographic: Traffic Jams Are Just One of the Problems Facing Climbers on Everest (2019)

versions.note: A very early start, to reach the summit before midday.

source.title: Alpine Ascents: Everest itinerary

facts.claim: The descent has the most accidents: exhaustion, cold, darkness, storms, oxygen running out, and climbers letting their guard down.

versions.note: The way back is dangerous and has the highest accident rate; fatigue, the weather and climbers letting their guard down add to the risk.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

versions.note: In 1996, Yasuko Namba died of exhaustion and cold just outside the South Col camp; on the north side, darkness and the blizzard trapped three Indian climbers on the way down.

source.title: Explorersweb: The 1996 Everest Tragedy, 30 Years Later

versions.note: Climbers going down have to wait in line too, unable to move fast enough to stay warm.

source.title: National Geographic: Traffic Jams Are Just One of the Problems Facing Climbers on Everest (2019)

versions.note: On the descent, the tube to his mask froze and shut off his oxygen.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Oxygen on Everest – Reviewing the Options

facts.claim: The summit is only halfway: keep the time, the strength and the oxygen for the way back to the South Col, and stay on guard to the end.

versions.note: Back to the South Col takes a little over 3 to 4 hours, and letting the guard down is one of the risks.

source.title: Hayden Rue: South Col of Mount Everest

versions.note: After the summit, the team goes back to the South Col and sleeps there, and goes down to Camp 2 the next day.

source.title: Alpine Ascents: Everest itinerary

versions.note: Turn back while there's oxygen enough to get down.

source.title: National Geographic: Traffic Jams Are Just One of the Problems Facing Climbers on Everest (2019)

facts.claim: Since the 2015 earthquake, the Hillary Step is a relatively steep snow slope, with the Kangshung Face on the right going up, under a cornice that can break.

versions.note: The traditional Hillary Step disappeared in the 2015 earthquake; today the route goes up a relatively steep snow slope with the Kangshung Face to the climber's right.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Summits and more missing climbers

versions.note: The route passes the former location of the Hillary Step, destroyed in a 2015 earthquake.

source.title: Mountain Project: Southeast Ridge (South Col) of Everest

versions.note: In 2024 a soft cornice overhanging the Kangshung Face broke at the Hillary Step under a line of climbers.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Weekend Update May 25: Season nears the End with Summits and Death

facts.claim: Before the 2015 earthquake, the Hillary Step was a vertical wall about this high, between the South Summit and the summit: the terrain of historical scenarios such as 1996.

versions.note: A 12 m high, vertical wall; the page has no date, and doesn't say what the wall is made of.

source.title: Olaf Rieck: Everest, the route

versions.note: The traditional Hillary Step disappeared in the 2015 earthquake; the page shows a photo of it before.

source.title: Alan Arnette: Everest 2024: Summits and more missing climbers

versions.note: In 1996, the ropes weren't fixed in time at the Hillary Step, and climbers waited in line below it.

source.title: Explorersweb: The 1996 Everest Tragedy, 30 Years Later

facts.question: What was the Hillary Step made of before 2015, rock, snow or both, and how high was it? The spec calls it a rock step; Olaf Rieck's undated page says only a 12 m vertical wall.
